Any writeup we can link on this type of attack?
Do you have access to openbmc-security@lists.ozlabs.org? If so, please search for "mTLS UPN domain suffix matching in bmcweb" (note, this is a part of the subject).

By the rules we try to keep those embargoed until we have a fix available that's been reviewed.  It's fine.

Yes, I have access to that and I don't understand the potential for attack.
If this is a common type of attack, please link some authority for it.

From my POV (and my teammates), it's not critical CVE indeed. Realistically, an attacker should have access to a trusted authority in order to be able to issue trusted certificate. A company might have multiple brands/domains (like macys.com and bloomingdales.com), should they use separated infra, while using the same certificate authority, an attacker may issue root@com certificate to access both of the realms.

> an attacker may issue root@com certificate to access both of the realms.

This reads like something made up to me.  Are there really companies that sign "com" as their hostname?
Why does this need to be configurable?  Why would someone choose each value?  Is there a default that we can agree on?

We want to avoid using TLDs and common top level domains.
The rational here is, 2 will work great for TLDs like .com, org, .edu (it will require user@domain.com, and fail for user@com). This is why it's a default. But it will still allow to use some common domains under country TLDs like (user@co.uk, user@com.au, etc), so if there is a company building their own image used only on hosts in such domains, they might want to increase this.

> fail for user@com

Isn't this invalid anyway?  "com" isn't a valid domain name?  Also, to hit this would require the certificate authority to sign a certificate with "user@com", right?  Why is that in the openbmc security domain?


> so if there is a company building their own image used only on hosts in such domains, they might want to increase this.

If the company is building their own image based on that host, it SHOULDN'T SIGN requests with a hostname that isn't recognized.  It's not bmcwebs job to police what hostnames are valid if the certificate authority has signed them, right?


Overall, I don't find the description of the option actionable.  A length check isn't a security boundary, especially if there are examples of domains that make no sense.

"user@com.au" would only be an issue if we're using a starts_with check, which I don't believe we are?

> Isn't this invalid anyway? "com" isn't a valid domain name?
Technically it's a valid domain. But it's irrelevant as the code does not do any "external" validity checks (like whether the domain name is registered), it treats it as a multi part string with dot as a delimiter.

> to hit this would require the certificate authority to sign a certificate with "user@com", right?
Right.

> Why is that in the openbmc security domain?
I don't have good answer on this question. "user@com" is not supposed to be valid/acceptable UPN. UPN comes from MS and not IETF standards, and tightly coupled with Active Directory, AD manages a forest of domains within *a company*, and UPN is a user @ one of those domains, so it cannot be user @ TLD. But this is not described by standards (at least I did not find anything about this).

Should bmcweb be responsible for enforcing this, I don't know. On the one hand I agree that adding lots of checks for corner cases will eventually make the code unnecessarily overcomplicated; OTOH validating user input is a good practice.

> it SHOULDN'T SIGN requests with a hostname that isn't recognized
It does not operate with host names, but domains and several layers of subdomains - it might be structured differently, like BU sales.example.com or region lhr.emea.example.com based scheme, and then users get UPN assigned depending on their level/structure - user@emea.example.com or user@example.com, hostnames follow the same scheme except host1.lhr.emea.example.com, host2.sfo.us-west.example.com. With UPN auth user@example.com will have access to both hosts, while user@emea.example.com only to the host1.lhr.emea.example.com one.

As I stated above, if company uses the same authority to issue certificates to multiple forest roots, attacker may issue TLD certificate. This change prevents BMCWeb from accepting certs with UPNs for TLDs. This configuration solves the problem of country TLDs like com.au.

> "user@com.au" would only be an issue if we're using a starts_with check, which I don't believe we are?

Do you mean ends_with?

---------------

This code is a little confusing to me.  Why are we parsing any of this?  Shouldn't the hostname on the BMC just be set correctly?  Why do we try to break this apart at all?

I explained the logic of UPN above - it should match hostnames in subdomains of the UPN domain. We cannot use ends_with as we want to ensure that the deepest domain part of the UPN domain also fully matchs, meaning if UPN is user@domain.com, so upn_domain_part is domain.com, it should match host.sub.domain.com, but should not match host.sub.mydomain.com, which would be the case with ends_with.

I'm not sure what to do here.  As much as people seem to care, they don't really seem to respond to comments on either binreapers patch (which needs a CLA) or this patch, and I'm not comfortable adding an option that's required for security, but I don't understand.  At this point LLMs are writing public hit articles claiming this isn't fixed, which I as a maintainer don't appreciate, but can't do much about.

https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/bmcweb/+/91337

Is my proposed fix to this.  If we need to, we can iterate further.  Please review if you are able.
